messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Klara was thirty-nine when the infection nearly killed her. A routine dental procedure had introduced bacteria into her bloodstream, and within days she was septic, lying in an ICU with tubes in her arms and a ventilator forcing air into her lungs. For two weeks she lay trapped under the fluorescent lights, unable to move, unable to speak, surrounded by the sharp, sweet smell of antiseptic and the beeping of monitors. In the worst moments, she truly believed she was dying, and that there was nothing she could do about it. When she finally recovered and went home, her body mended, but something in her mind did not.

Months later, the world still felt dangerous. Klara returned to her dental practice, but the familiar smell of disinfectant in her own operatory made her stomach clench. Each time she caught a whiff of antiseptic, the thought that she was weak returned, along with the certainty that her body had betrayed her and could never be trusted again. She began to notice old photos of herself from before the illness—snapshots of a woman who had not known helplessness—and she felt a sharp gap between that person and the one she was now. That person had been whole; this person felt permanently damaged, changed for the worse. The feeling of entrapment, of having no options, resurfaced whenever she was in a crowded room or even in her small clinic, and it whispered that she was too fragile to handle even ordinary life.

Because Klara believed she was weak and that her body was unreliable, she started avoiding anything that might confirm those beliefs. She stopped looking at her own body in the mirror, turning away when she undressed, afraid she would see evidence of damage. She avoided talking to her partner about the illness, refusing to say the word “sepsis” even when he asked, because speaking about it made the weakness feel real. She also began to avoid other people, declining invitations and leaving social gatherings early, certain that they could see she was not the same person—that she was broken. Every time she avoided, the conviction grew stronger. Her silence about the illness deepened her sense of permanent change; by not talking, she confirmed to herself that there was something unspeakable wrong.

The cycle tightened. Her view of herself as damaged made her more sensitive to triggers. She began to scan her environment for hospital smells, and when she found them—even in a hand sanitizer at the grocery store—the sense of entrapment flooded back, and she felt weak all over again. At work, she started avoiding certain dental procedures that required strong antiseptics, delegating them to her assistant or rescheduling patients. This avoidance felt like a compromise, but it also felt like defeat. Her partner noticed her distance and grew frustrated; she could not explain why she could not talk, and his irritation only confirmed to her that she had become a different, lesser person. She began to feel trapped not just in her memories but in her own life, with no options to escape the loop.

What finally brought Klara to therapy was a panic attack in her dental operatory. A patient came in with a mouth infection, and the combination of the odor, the feeling of being enclosed in the small room, and the thought that she had no control over her own safety sent her heart racing. She excused herself to the bathroom, where she could not stop shaking. That night she told her partner she needed help. She is afraid that therapy will only confirm what she already believes—that she is broken, that the damage is permanent—but she is also desperate to feel normal again, to trust her body, to not flinch at a smell. She wants to believe there is a way out, even though she cannot see it yet.
